name: Genetic fallacy
statement: Judging a claim by where it came from is listed as a fallacy, and industry-sponsored drug studies report favourable results more often, RR 1.27.
meaning: Two complaints travel under the name. Cohen and Nagel used it for confusion between the history of a theory and the logical analysis of its structure. Their section sets out two errors of that kind: deducing what must have happened from logic alone, and letting an account of how a science grew stand in for an analysis of how its propositions hang together. The popular sense is narrower and is about dismissal. A claim is rejected because of who made it, what motive produced it, or where it came from. Cohen and Nagel handled that move as well, eight pages earlier and under a different heading, and they drew a line most retellings drop. Motives, they wrote, bear on the credibility of a witness reporting what he has observed, and not on whether premises suffice to demonstrate a conclusion. That line is the whole of the subject. Where a listener is asked to take a premise on somebody's word, the source's reliability is part of the evidence for the premise. Where the argument is set out in full, its origin adds nothing to it. The atlas covers the personal case under ad hominem and the persuasion case under source bias. This entry takes origin in general, and the asymmetry between using one to support a claim and using one to sink it.

origin.who: Morris R. Cohen and Ernest Nagel
origin.where: An Introduction to Logic and Scientific Method
origin.note: The heading 'The Genetic Fallacy' appears in the chapter on fallacies, in the section on abuses of scientific method, and the book's own index gives it pages 388 to 390. What it names there is not dismissal by source. Form one 'takes a logical for a temporal order', the a priori reconstruction of history from what primitive man 'must have done'. Form two is 'the converse error', that 'an actual history of any science, art, or social institution can take the place of a logical analysis of its structure'. Neither mentions rejecting a claim because of its origin. That argument sits on pages 380 to 381 under the argumentum ad hominem, where the authors write that after 'popular psychoanalysis' any argument 'can be refuted in this way by inventing some unfavorable psychogenetic account of how or why the proponent of the argument came to hold that view'. Read in the Routledge and Kegan Paul complete edition, first published in England in 1934, in a later reprint scanned by the Internet Archive. Whether Cohen and Nagel coined the term could not be settled. Klement dates its introduction to 'probably in the 1920s or 1930s' and refers the history to Crouch's 1993 paper, which was not obtained.

evidence:
Nothing measured carries the name. A Europe PMC search for the exact phrase returns 23 records, all of them essays and commentary in bioethics, psychoanalysis and science education, and none an experiment. The measurable version of the question is whether people discount a claim for its origin, and by how much against how much the origin is worth.

Origin is worth something, and the size is known for one case. Lundh and colleagues' Cochrane methodology review pooled 75 papers comparing industry-sponsored drug and device studies with studies funded otherwise. Industry-sponsored studies more often had favourable efficacy results, RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.37, from 25 papers, and more often had favourable conclusions, RR 1.34, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.51, from 29 papers. They also agreed less often with their own results, RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.98, from six papers, and were no worse on sequence generation, allocation concealment, follow-up or selective outcome reporting. They were better on blinding, RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.50. The authors conclude that the association survives standard risk-of-bias assessment.

Whether readers apply a discount of the right size has been tested by randomising the disclosure. Kesselheim and colleagues sent 503 board-certified internists abstracts of hypothetical trials, each written at high, medium or low methodologic rigor and carrying one of three statements: pharmaceutical funding, NIH funding, or none. Of those invited 269 responded, a 53.5% rate, and 263 answered every question for at least one abstract. Rigor registered. Against a medium-rigor trial, a high-rigor one was more often called rigorous, odds ratio 3.95, 95% CI 2.81 to 5.55, P<0.001, and a low-rigor one less often, odds ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.76, P<0.001. Disclosed industry funding, against no disclosure, lowered the odds of calling a trial rigorous to 0.63, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.87, P = 0.006. It lowered confidence in the results to 0.71, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.98, P = 0.04, and willingness to prescribe to 0.68, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.94, P = 0.02. Against an NIH-funded trial the willingness ratio was 0.52, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.71, P<0.001. The prescribing penalty was the same at every level of rigor, P = 0.87 comparing high with medium and P = 0.83 comparing low with medium. The authors write that such scepticism 'can also reduce the credibility and acceptance of even high-quality research that is industry-supported'.

Two later randomised trials found no such discount. Tijdink, Smulders, Bouter and Vinkers randomised 395 Dutch psychiatrists to one of four versions of an abstract for a fictitious antipsychotic trial, crossing funding disclosure with a positive or negative outcome. Credibility on a 10-point scale was 4.64 with the disclosure and 4.76 without, mean difference 0.12, and clinical relevance 5.30 against 5.16, mean difference 0.14. Methodological quality scored 38.65 against 38.87 and interest in reading the article 4.51 against 4.65. The same respondents did discriminate on outcome: a negative result was rated 5.10 for credibility against 4.29 for a positive one, mean difference 0.81, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.18. Buffel du Vaure, Boutron, Perrodeau and Ravaud gave 354 French general practitioners abstracts of real industry-funded trials in three formats, 118 per arm, varying only whether the funding source and the authors' conflicts were printed. Confidence in the conclusions moved 0.2, 95% CI -0.6 to 1.0, P = 0.84, for funding alone against neither, and -0.6, 95% CI -1.5 to 0.2, P = 0.15, for funding plus conflicts against funding alone.

Silverman and colleagues found the discount depends on whether a comparison is available. They gave 253 responding Fellows of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists a single positive abstract for a fictitious drug under one of three conflict conditions. Self-reported prescribing likelihood did not shift. Asked afterwards to compare conflict with no conflict directly, 69% said they would discount for a researcher conflict and 57% for a presenter conflict. The paper is quoted here from its PubMed abstract.

On how origin should be weighed, Hahn, Harris and Corner ran two experiments in which reliability and content were crossed. In the first, 97 sixth-form students in South Wales rated four dialogues built on absent evidence, with the claim carried either by the journal Science or by a circular email, and supported by either one experiment or fifty. Both mattered, source F(1, 384) = 247.72, p < .001, and evidence F(1, 384) = 101.71, p < .001, and so did their interaction, F(1, 384) = 7.91, p < .01. In the second, 120 Cardiff undergraduates read a claim about an energy drink from a consumer watchdog or from spam, at three strengths. Source gave F(1, 114) = 5.35, evidence F(2, 114) = 25.53 and the interaction F(2, 114) = 16.16. Reliability changed nothing when the evidence was strong, F(1, 114) = 1.87, or very weak, F(1, 114) = 3.44, and mattered in between, F(1, 114) = 12.36. The authors read the multiplicative pattern as what a Bayesian account predicts.

Klement's analysis of when genetic reasoning is legitimate supplies the asymmetry. Arguing that a belief is true because it was produced by a reliable process is inductively strong. Arguing that a belief is false because it was produced by an unreliable process is not, because an unreliable process is merely no better than chance, and defeating the claim needs a process that is 'anti-reliable', likelier to yield falsehoods than truths. Such processes exist and are rare. So origin supports a claim more readily than it sinks one.

replication.headline: One randomised trial found physicians discounting a study for its industry funding at every level of study quality. Two later randomised trials, on 395 psychiatrists and 354 general practitioners, found no effect of the same disclosure.
replication.detail: Kesselheim and colleagues reported that disclosed industry funding cut the odds of a trial being called rigorous to 0.63, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.87, and the odds of willingness to prescribe to 0.68, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.94, in 269 internists. Tijdink and colleagues name that study as the contrast for their own null and offer two explanations for the gap, the different design and a possible difference between internists and psychiatrists. Their credibility means were 4.64 with disclosure and 4.76 without on a 10-point scale, and the same participants separated a negative from a positive outcome by 0.81, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.18, so the null is not a failure of the instrument to move at all. Buffel du Vaure and colleagues, powered to detect an effect size of 0.5, put the confidence difference at 0.2, 95% CI -0.6 to 1.0, for disclosing the funding source. Their abstracts all described industry-funded trials, so the manipulation was disclosure rather than sponsorship. Silverman and colleagues suggest a moderator that would reconcile the set: physicians did not discount a conflicted study read on its own, and a majority said they would discount when asked to compare a conflicted study with an unconflicted one. Two of the three intervals printed in Tijdink's Table 2 for the funding contrast are not centred on the mean difference they accompany, and they are reproduced above as printed rather than corrected.

study.cite: Tijdink, J. K., Smulders, Y. M., Bouter, L. M., & Vinkers, C. H. (2019). The effects of industry funding and positive outcomes in the interpretation of clinical trial results: a randomized trial among Dutch psychiatrists. BMC Medical Ethics, 20, 66.

limits:
The pooled figure and the reader experiments measure different things and no source compares them. Lundh's risk ratios describe how often sponsored studies report favourable results; Kesselheim's odds ratios describe how far a rating moves on a survey. Converting one into a test of whether the other is the right size would produce a number that appears in no document, so no such comparison is made here.

The disclosure trials all use written abstracts and self-reported intentions. Kesselheim's own limitations note that respondents reacted to hypothetical trials of three new drugs, whereas real prescribing integrates many sources, and that unmeasured differences between responders and non-responders may bias the sample. Tijdink's response rate is 45% of psychiatrists who opened the email and 25% of the 1,566 invited. Silverman's paper was not obtained and everything attributed to it here comes from its PubMed abstract, including the 69% and 57%.

Crouch's 1993 history of the term, which Klement cites for the question of who introduced it, was not obtained; its Crossref record carries no abstract. Goudge's 1961 Synthese paper and Hanson's 1967 survey of formulations were likewise not obtained. The claim sometimes made that Mortimer Adler used 'the fallacy of genetic interpretation' in 1926 was not traced to any document read here, and it is left out for that reason.

Lewis's 'Bulverism' was not read in its own printing. The passage quoted below is taken from Sarot's article in HTS Teologiese Studies, which quotes it at page 20 of the Collins edition of Compelling Reason and dates the essay to 1941. The reported first appearance in Time and Tide on 29 March 1941, and the longer version read to the Oxford Socratic Club in February 1944 and printed in the Socratic Digest, could not be confirmed against either publication.

Searches ran over Crossref by bibliographic query, Europe PMC by exact phrase, OpenAlex, PubMed, PubMed Central and general web search. The Stanford Encyclopedia's survey of fallacies was fetched in full and searched for the string 'genetic', which returned nothing, so the fallacy is not treated there under that name.
misreadings:
The commonest error is the one the textbook definition invites, that an origin is irrelevant to truth. Klement shows the schemes it would condemn. If a belief that the cat is on the mat was caused by the cat's being on the mat, its causal history guarantees its truth. If it came from a reliable belief-forming process, its history makes it probably true. Neither argument is fallacious, and both are genetic.

The error has a mirror image worth avoiding too. Klement's asymmetry says that discovering an unreliable origin does not make a belief false, because an unreliable process is one that is no better than chance, and 'even magic eight-balls provide the right answer half of the time'. Knocking a claim down by its origin needs an 'anti-reliable' process, one that produces falsehoods more often than truths, and those are hard to find.

The founding text is misdescribed. Cohen and Nagel's genetic fallacy is about the relation between a history and a logical structure, and their examples are speculative reconstructions of prehistory and histories of science offered in place of analysis. The dismissal-by-origin move appears in the same chapter under the argumentum ad hominem, where they allow that motives bear on a witness's credibility while denying that they bear on the force of an argument. A retelling that credits them with naming the modern fallacy is describing the wrong section.

Bulverism is treated as another word for it. Lewis's target is narrower. Sarot quotes him imagining Ezekiel Bulver, whose destiny was fixed at five when he heard his mother tell his father 'Oh, you say that because you are a man', and who then grasped 'the great truth that refutation is no necessary part of argument. Assume that your opponent is wrong, and then explain his error, and the world will be at your feet'. What Lewis names is the order of operations, explaining an error before establishing that it is one. That is a charge about a debating habit rather than about the relevance of origins.

Calling the funding discount a fallacy is the applied version of the same mistake. Sponsorship predicts the result, RR 1.27 for favourable efficacy findings and RR 1.34 for favourable conclusions, so weighing it is not irrelevance. What Kesselheim's physicians did that is harder to defend is apply the same penalty regardless of the rigor described in front of them, P = 0.87 and P = 0.83 across rigor levels, and rate the described design itself as less rigorous.

The reader evidence is quoted more confidently than it holds. Two randomised trials after Kesselheim found no effect of disclosure at all, and Silverman found physicians discounting only when a comparison was in view. Anyone citing the genetic fallacy as an established finding about doctors is citing one of three trials.
